notes:
Now let me compose the verse-by-verse notes from what I have gathered. I have detailed content from Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic), Gill's Exposition (older Baptist), Ellicott's Commentary (Anglican), Matthew Henry's Commentary (Puritan/Reformed), JFB (Reformed Presbyterian), and excerpts from Clarke (Methodist) and the Pulpit Commentary.

---

# Psalm 10 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview

Psalm 10 is a lament about the apparent prosperity and success of the wicked alongside God's seeming inaction. It has no title in the Hebrew, leading the Septuagint (LXX) to join it with Psalm 9 as a single psalm. However, the Hebrew tradition keeps them separate, and "the scope and style are certainly different" (Matthew Henry). Martin Luther judged that "there is not, in my judgment, a Psalm which describes the mind, the manners, the works, the words, the feelings, and the fate of the ungodly with so much propriety, fullness, and light, as this Psalm" (cited in Spurgeon, via Enduring Word).

The psalm moves from anguished questioning (v. 1) to calm confidence in God's eternal reign (v. 16). The emphasis is "the problem of theodicy, the justice of God in the face of the prosperity of wicked Israelites. Like the Book of Job, the psalm does not resolve the problem but refocuses on God (Psalms 10:14)" (Dr. Constable, studylight.org).

Structurally: vv. 1–11 describe the wicked; vv. 12–18 are prayer and confident assertion.

---

## v. 1 — "Why, O LORD, do You stand far off? Why do You hide in times of trouble?"

**Traditional reading:** The psalmist opens not by complaining of the trouble itself but of God's felt absence during it. Matthew Henry writes, "God's withdrawings are very grievous to his people at any time, but especially in times of trouble. Outward deliverance is afar off and is hidden from us, and then we think God is afar off … we stand afar off from God by our unbelief, and then we complain that God stands afar off from us." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/10.htm)

Spurgeon adds: "The presence of God is the joy of his people, but any suspicion of his absence is distracting beyond measure.... It is not the trouble, but the hiding of our Father's face, which cuts us to the quick." (Cited in enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-10/)

Gill notes that God "by his infinite essence and power is everywhere," so "standing afar off" refers to the *withdrawal of gracious presence* — when God defers help and does not immediately come to visit His people. This is "consistent with his everlasting and unchangeable love to them, but is what fills them with grief and sorrow." (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/10.htm)

Ellicott notes that "times of trouble" translates a rare Hebrew word used only here and in Psalm 9:9; Maclaren explains it as "a cutting off, i.e., of hope of deliverance. The notion of distress intensified to despair is conveyed." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/10.htm)

**Tradition note — Reformed / Baptist:** Gill characteristically applies the psalm prophetically to "antichrist and antichristian times," seeing the "times of trouble" as the persecution era under the Papacy during the church's wilderness period (the 1,260 days/years). This historicist reading is typical of older Baptist and Protestant commentators. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/10.htm)

---

## v. 2 — "In pride the wicked pursue the needy; let them be caught in the schemes they devise."

**Traditional reading:** The proud wicked man persecutes (or "hotly pursues," as the Hebrew verb implies — Genesis 31:36) the poor/afflicted. Matthew Henry calls pride and persecution "the two heads of the charge" against the wicked — "the former the cause of the latter. Proud men will have all about them to be of their mind … and those that either eclipse them or will not yield to them they malign and hate." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/10.htm)

The second clause ("let them be caught") is a prayer, though in other psalms (e.g., Psalm 9:15) it is a confident expectation. Enduring Word notes: "There are none who will dispute the justice of God, when he shall hang every Haman on his own gallows, and cast all the enemies of his Daniels into their own den of lions" (Spurgeon). (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-10/)

**Text-critical note (Ellicott):** Ellicott argues the first clause is better translated "in the pride of the wicked, the sufferer burns" (following LXX, Aquila, Symmachus, and Vulgate) — meaning the afflictions the sufferer endures, not indignation. The second clause, he suggests, should have the sufferers as subject: "they (the sufferers) are taken in the plot which they (the wicked) have devised." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/10.htm)

---

## v. 3 — "For the wicked man boasts in the cravings of his heart; he blesses the greedy and reviles the LORD."

**Traditional reading:** The wicked "speaketh praise to the lust of his soul" (Ellicott's literal rendering) — he congratulates himself on his evil desires. Matthew Henry: "The sinner proudly glories in his power and success. He boasts of his heart's desire, boasts that he can do what he pleases … and that he has all he wished for." He also "blesses the covetous, whom the Lord abhors" — "see how God and men differ in their sentiments of persons." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/10.htm)

**Text-critical note (Ellicott):** Ellicott notes that "blesseth" is actually "curseth" by a common Hebrew euphemism (compare 1 Kings 21:23; Job 1:5). The word for "covetous" properly means "robber." He offers several possible syntactical readings, the best being: "he greedily curses, despises Jehovah." The LXX and Vulgate read: "The wicked is praised; the sinner has irritated the Lord." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/10.htm)

---

## v. 4 — "In his pride the wicked man does not seek Him; in all his schemes there is no God."

**Traditional reading:** This verse diagnoses the root of the wicked man's sin: his proud refusal to seek God. Enduring Word explains: "Men do not seek God; this is a great sin. Men do not think about God; this also is a great sin. Man has obligations to God as His Creator and sovereign, and it is a sin to neglect them. Man commits these sins because of his proud countenance; ignoring God is an expression of our independence and perceived equality (or superiority) to Him." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-10/)

Matthew Henry: "The wicked, through the pride of his countenance … will not seek after God, nor entertain the thoughts of him. God is not in all his thoughts, not in any of them. All his thoughts are that there is not God." He adds that the cause is pride: "Men will not seek after God because they think they have no need of him, their own hands are sufficient for them." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/10.htm)

**Text-critical note (Ellicott):** Ellicott says the Authorised Version "has quite missed the meaning of this verse." He translates: "the wicked in his haughtiness (literally, height of his nostril — comp. 'to turn up one's nose at a person') saith He will not requite it (i.e., punish; comp. v. 13). There is no God in all his thought." So the "not seeking" is actually a denial that God will call him to account. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/10.htm)

**Tradition note — Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):** David Guzik makes the striking observation that although "God is in none of his thoughts," the wicked man "cannot not think of God, as he does later in vv. 11 and 13 (the thoughts, God has forgotten; He hides His face; He will never see…). Try as he may, he can't stop thinking about God." This psychological insight is characteristic of the application-oriented Pentecostal reading. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-10/)

---

## v. 5 — "He is secure in his ways at all times; Your lofty judgments are far from him; he sneers at all his foes."

**Traditional reading:** The wicked man appears to prosper continually. Enduring Word notes the psalmist's protest: "not only did the wicked man seem to enjoy constant prosperity, but he did so because God's judgments are far above, out of his sight." The thought is: "If only God would demonstrate His judgment to this wicked man, he would change his ways." Yet this is less complaint than confidence — "the psalmist recognized that the wicked could never prosper unless God allowed it; so he appealed to God to not allow it." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-10/)

**Text-critical note (Ellicott):** "His ways are always grievous" is better rendered "his enterprises always succeed" (from Job 20:21). Or "his ways are always strong" implying the bold, reckless course of a tyrant (compare Psalm 73:12). "Puffeth" means to snort in scorn — after describing the wicked with "his nose high in the air," the word is "especially forcible." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/10.htm)

Matthew Henry: "He proudly makes light of God's commandments and judgments … God's judgments … are far above out of his sight; he is not sensible of his duty by the law of God nor of his danger by the wrath and curse of God." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/10.htm)

---

## v. 6 — "He says to himself, 'I will not be moved; from age to age I am free of distress.'"

**Traditional reading:** The wicked man's false security — he imagines his prosperity will last forever. Matthew Henry: "He hath said in his heart, and pleased himself with the thought, I shall not be moved … like Babylon, that said, I shall be a lady for ever … Those are nearest ruin who thus set it furthest from them." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/10.htm)

**Text-critical note (Ellicott):** The Hebrew construction is involved. Literally: "I shall not be moved to generation and generation, which not in evil." The best rendering: "I shall never be moved at any time: I who am without ill." The LXX and Vulgate omit the relative altogether. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/10.htm)

---

## v. 7 — "His mouth is full of cursing, deceit, and violence; trouble and malice are under his tongue."

**Traditional reading:** The wicked man's speech reveals his heart. Boice (cited in Enduring Word): "Cursing, lying, threatening, and troubling and evil speech are all destructive. They flow from one who does not believe that God will hold him or her accountable." Trapp: "Such cursing men are cursed men." Clarke: "What a finished character! A blasphemer, a deceitful man, and a knave!" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-10/)

Matthew Henry: "Where there is a heart full of malice there is commonly a mouth full of curses." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/10.htm)

Ellicott notes the link between "cursing" and "deceit" suggests perjury (compare Hosea 4:2, "swearing and lying"). (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/10.htm)

---

## vv. 8–9 — "He lies in wait near the villages; in ambush he slays the innocent … he lurks to seize the oppressed; he catches the lowly in his net."

**Traditional reading:** The psalmist piles up images of predatory violence — the wicked man as a lurking murderer (v. 8) and then as a lion and a hunter/fowler (v. 9). Enduring Word stresses two key traits: (a) **secrecy** — "lurking places … secret places … eyes are secretly fixed … lies in wait secretly … he lies low"; (b) **bullying the weak** — "he isn't manful or honorable enough to openly fight those who might effectively fight back." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-10/)

Matthew Henry: "Those are perfectly lost to all honesty and honour against whose mischievous designs neither innocence nor poverty will be any man's security." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/10.htm)

Ellicott notes the "confusion of metaphor" — first the lion watching for prey, then the hunter snaring animals — and points out the rare Hebrew word for "poor" (occurring three times in this psalm: vv. 8, 10, 14) with the root idea of "darkness," hence "obscure, humble." Symmachus renders it "feeble." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/10.htm)

**Older Baptist note (Gill):** Gill reads v. 8 as describing the Pope and cardinals — "Antichrist sits in the temple of God, and by his emissaries gets into the villages, the particular churches and congregations of saints, where they lie in ambush to do mischief." The "secret places" refer to private massacres or the Inquisition. The lion in v. 9 is the "first beast in Revelation 13:2 … said to have a mouth like a lion." This thoroughgoing identification with the Papacy is characteristic of historic Protestant (especially Baptist) interpretation. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/10.htm)

---

## v. 10 — "They are crushed and beaten down; the hapless fall prey to his strength."

**Traditional reading:** The wicked man crouches low like a beast before springing — the result: the helpless are crushed. Matthew Henry notes this crouching also implies hypocrisy: "They cover their malicious designs with the pretence of meekness and humility … they seem to humble themselves to take cognizance of the poor … when it is in order to make them fall." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/10.htm)

**Text-critical note (Ellicott):** Instead of "croucheth," some (Jerome, Perowne, Syriac) render "is crushed," making the sufferer the subject. Alternatively, keeping the sense of "darkness": "he crouches and skulks, and lies darkly down in his strong places." "By his strong ones" — possibly "by his strong claws," recurring to the lion metaphor. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/10.htm)

Kidner (cited in Enduring Word) notes that the "helpless" (or "hapless," "poor wretch," NEB) is "a word only found in this psalm (vv. 8, 10, 14), which has received various explanations, but is probably derived from a root meaning to be black, and hence comes to mean miserable, hapless." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-10/)

---

## v. 11 — "He says to himself, 'God has forgotten; He hides His face and never sees.'"

**Traditional reading:** This is the theological rationale behind the wicked man's crimes. He persuades himself that God is indifferent or blind. Enduring Word calls this "blasphemy against God" added to his sins against mankind. Stephen Charnock (cited in Spurgeon): "Is it not a senseless thing to be careless of sins committed long ago? The old sins forgotten by men, stick fast in an infinite understanding. Time cannot raze out that which hath been known from eternity." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-10/)

Enduring Word also highlights the contrast: the believer in v. 1 *fears* God has forgotten (and it causes pain); the sinner in v. 11 *hopes* God has forgotten (and takes false comfort). Pride makes him "misread God's patience as inaction." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-10/)

Matthew Henry says this is "a blasphemous reproach" upon three attributes of God: (1) His omniscience and providence — as if He could not or did not see; (2) His holiness — as if He did not dislike the vilest crimes; (3) His justice — as if He would never reckon with the wicked. (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/10.htm)

---

## v. 12 — "Arise, O LORD! Lift up Your hand, O God! Do not forget the helpless."

**Traditional reading:** The turning point. After the long description of wickedness, the psalmist cries for action. Matthew Henry: "'Arise, O Lord! O God! lift up thy hand, manifest thy presence and providence in the affairs of this lower world. … Manifest thy power, exert it for the maintaining of thy own cause, lift up thy hand to give a fatal blow to these oppressors; let thy everlasting arm be made bare.'" (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/10.htm)

Enduring Word speculates (since the psalm is untitled but surrounded by Davidic psalms) that David may have written this during Saul's persecution — David, though a warrior, would not lift his hand against "the LORD's anointed," so he cries for God to act instead. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-10/)

Ellicott notes that here "the acrostic arrangement is resumed with *koph*" — the broken acrostic that spans Psalms 9–10. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/10.htm)

---

## v. 13 — "Why has the wicked man renounced God? He says to himself, 'You will never call me to account.'"

**Traditional reading:** The psalmist answers his own question: the wicked renounces God because he believes in impunity. Horne (cited in Enduring Word): "The long-suffering of God, instead of leading such a one to repentance, only hardens him in his iniquity. Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, he thinks it will not be executed at all." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-10/)

Matthew Henry marvels at two things: (1) "At the wickedness of the wicked: 'Why do they speak so impiously, why so absurdly?'" and (2) "At the patience and forbearance of God towards them: 'Why are they suffered thus to contemn God? Why does he not immediately vindicate himself and take vengeance on them?'" His answer: "It is because the day of reckoning is yet to come, when the measure of their iniquity is full." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/10.htm)

---

## v. 14 — "But You have regarded trouble and grief; You see to repay it by Your hand. The victim entrusts himself to You; You are the helper of the fatherless."

**Traditional reading:** The great "but" — the turning point of faith. Against the wicked man's claim that God does not see, the psalmist asserts: God does see, and not only sees but will *repay*. Enduring Word calls this "the confidence of the psalmist in God's judgments. He most certainly will repay the wicked for their sins." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-10/)

Matthew Henry elaborates: "'Do the persecutors encourage themselves with a groundless fancy that thou wilt never see it? Let the persecuted encourage themselves with a well-grounded faith, not only that thou hast seen it, but that thou doest behold it … nay, not only thou hast seen it and dost behold it, but thou wilt requite it, wilt recompense it into their bosoms, by thy just and avenging hand.'" (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/10.htm)

**Reformed note (Dr. Constable):** The problem of theodicy "does not resolve the problem but refocuses on God (Psalms 10:14)." The answer to "why do the wicked prosper?" is not a philosophical explanation but a person — God who sees and will act. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-10.html)

---

## v. 15 — "Break the arm of the wicked and evildoer; call him to account for his wickedness until none is left to be found."

**Traditional reading:** A bold imprecatory prayer. Matthew Henry explains two requests: (1) "That he would disable them from doing any mischief: Break thou the arm of the wicked, take away his power"; (2) "That he would deal with them for the mischief they had done: 'Seek out his wickedness; let that be all brought to light … bring it out till thou find none, that is, till none of his evil deeds remain unreckoned for.'" He adds the hope that God might take away dominion but prolong life, as in Daniel 7:12, "that they might have time to repent." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/10.htm)

**Text-critical note (Ellicott):** The construction is difficult. The first clause should end at "wicked," with "and the evil" being absolute. Translate: "and as for the evil man, thou shalt look for his wickedness, and not find it" — a proverbial expression for riddance of evil (compare Psalm 37:36; Isaiah 41:12). The LXX reads: "his sin shall be sought, and not be found." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/10.htm)

Dr. Constable notes that the Hebrew word translated "seek out" or "call to account" here is the same word rendered "requires blood" or "avenges" in Psalm 9:12 — linking the two psalms. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-10.html)

---

## v. 16 — "The LORD is King forever and ever; the nations perish from His land."

**Traditional reading:** The psalm reaches its theological climax. Enduring Word: "The psalmist began with almost despair in his times of trouble; he ends with calm confidence in the reign of the LORD as an eternal King." God had been declared King of Israel since Exodus 15:18, even when His people rejected His rule (1 Samuel 8:7–9). (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-10/)

Matthew Henry reads "the nations perish from His land" as recalling the conquest of Canaan — "the remainders of the Canaanites, the seven devoted nations … are now, at length, utterly rooted out; and this is an encouragement to us to hope that God will, in like manner, break the arm of the oppressive Israelites, who were, in some respects, worse than heathens." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/10.htm)

**Reformed/Presbyterian (JFB):** "God reigns. The wicked, if for a time successful, shall be cut off. He hears and confirms the hearts of His suffering people (Ps 112:7), executes justice for the feeble, and represses the pride and violence of conceited, though frail, men." (biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/psalms/10.htm)

Ellicott: "If the psalm has hitherto been personal, it here swells out into a larger strain of national hope and faith." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/10.htm)

---

## v. 17 — "You have heard, O LORD, the desire of the humble; You will strengthen their hearts. You will incline Your ear…"

**Traditional reading:** The psalmist expresses confidence that God hears. Spurgeon (cited in Enduring Word): "David does not say, 'Thou hast heard the prayer of the humble;' he means that, but he also means a great deal more. Sometimes, we have desires that we cannot express; they are too big, too deep; we cannot clothe them in language. … the Lord hears the desire when we cannot or dare not turn it into the actual form of a prayer." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-10/)

The phrase "You will strengthen [prepare] their hearts" (BSB: "strengthen"; traditional: "prepare") is a major teaching point. Spurgeon: "Surely none but the Lord can prepare a heart for prayer. One old writer says it is far harder work to raise the big bell into the steeple than to ring it afterwards. … When the bell is well hung you can ring it readily enough; but in that uplifting of the heart lies the work and the labor." Trapp: "Where God giveth a praying heart it is sure that he will show a pitying heart. If he prepare the heart, he will also bend his ear." Clarke: "See the economy of the grace of God: 1. God prepares the heart; 2. Suggests the prayer; 3. Hears what is prayed; 4. Answers the petition. He who has got a cry in his heart after God, may rest assured that that cry proceeded from a Divine preparation." (All cited in enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-10/)

Matthew Henry draws out the method: "He first prepares the heart of his people and then gives them an answer of peace … God's working upon us is the best earnest of his working for us." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/10.htm)

**Tradition note — Pentecostal/Charismatic:** The emphasis on God "preparing the heart" as a supernatural act preceding prayer resonates strongly with Pentecostal theology of divine initiative. Enduring Word's David Guzik notes it is "a great gift, an answer to prayer, and a mark of God's blessing." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-10/)

---

## v. 18 — "to vindicate the fatherless and oppressed, that the men of the earth may strike terror no more."

**Traditional reading:** The psalm ends with the assurance of God's justice. Matthew Henry: "He will put an end to the fury of the persecutors. Hitherto they shall come, but no further; here shall the proud waves of their malice be stayed." He notes the phrase "the man of the earth" is contemptuous — "a man out of the earth … sprung out of the earth, and therefore mean, and weak, and hastening to the earth again. Why then should we be afraid of the fury of the oppressor when he is but man that shall die, a son of man that shall be as grass? He that protects us is the Lord of heaven; he that persecutes us is but a man of the earth." (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/10.htm)

Poole (cited in Enduring Word): the phrase means "earthly and mortal men, who are made of the dust, and must return to it, such as the oppressors of the people are." Morgan: "Under the rule of God, the day must come when, 'That man who is of the earth may be terrible no more.' These were the concluding words of the song, and they constitute a fitting answer to its opening inquiry." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-10/)

**Text-critical note (Ellicott):** The literal Hebrew is "that may not continue to terrify (or defy) mere man from the earth." He suggests it echoes Psalm 9:20, where the word is used contemptuously of the "heathen" — "That the nations from the earth (i.e., spread over the earth) may know themselves to be but men, and no longer defy Israel and Israel's God." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/10.htm)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**Baptist (historic, Gill):** Gill reads the entire psalm as a prophetic description of Antichrist — the Pope and the Roman Catholic system. The "wicked" is "the man of sin, and son of perdition, antichrist, the great persecutor of Christ's poor saints." The "lurking places of the villages" are local churches infiltrated by papal emissaries; the "net" is the allurements of riches, honours, and lying wonders. This anti-papal reading was standard among early Protestants (Luther, Calvin, the translators of the Geneva Bible) but is now largely confined to certain conservative Baptist and Reformed circles. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/10.htm)

**Reformed/Presbyterian (Matthew Henry, JFB):** The emphasis falls on God's sovereignty. Even when God appears absent, He is "King forever and ever." The psalm is read as a study in divine providence — God's delay is not neglect but patience, "because the day of reckoning is yet to come, when the measure of their iniquity is full." The "theodicy" question (why do the wicked prosper?) is answered by refocusing on God's character rather than by philosophical explanation. (biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/10.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/psalms/10.htm)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Strong emphasis on personal application, spiritual warfare, and the preparation of the heart as a supernatural gift. The wicked man's internal psychology receives extended attention — he "can't stop thinking about God" despite his denial. The movement from despair to confident faith is seen as a paradigm for the believer's experience. The commentary is markedly more experiential and devotional than academic. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-10/)

**Anglican (Ellicott):** Ellicott gives the most attention to textual and translational issues — the LXX's joining of Psalms 9–10, the broken acrostic, alternative readings from Aquila, Symmachus, Jerome, and the Vulgate. He offers the most defensible English renderings based on Hebrew syntax. His approach is scholarly and text-critical rather than homiletical. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/10.htm)

**Methodist/Wesleyan (Clarke):** Clarke's overview (preserved on biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/psalms/10.htm) focuses on the moral character of the wicked — "a blasphemer, a deceitful man, and a knave!" — and on the "economy of the grace of God" in v. 17: God prepares the heart, suggests the prayer, hears it, and answers. This emphasis on the ordo salutis (order of salvation) and divine-human cooperation reflects Wesleyan concerns. Clarke also applies v. 16 optimistically to his own nation: "Once it was entirely heathen; now not one heathen family in the whole land" (speaking of England).

**Lutheran:** Martin Luther himself praised this psalm as unparalleled in its description of the ungodly (cited in Spurgeon/Enduring Word). Lutheran commentators typically note the distinction between Law (the exposure of sin in vv. 1–11) and Gospel (the declaration of God's gracious action in vv. 14–18). The specific Lutheran source (lcms.org or 1517.org) could not be retrieved within search limits.

---

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship / NET Bible notes:** The psalm is an acrostic poem (along with Psalm 9), with its stanzas beginning with successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet. This structural feature links the two psalms and explains why the LXX considered them one composition. The broken acrostic pattern (some letters missing or out of order) may reflect textual transmission issues or deliberate artistic choice. (This is standard in modern commentaries; the NET Bible notes on Psalm 10 could not be fetched within limits.)

**Catholic / Orthodox:** Catholic and Orthodox readings (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org) could not be retrieved within the search and fetch limits. However, it is well known that the Vulgate and Septuagint traditions join Psalms 9 and 10 into a single psalm (Psalm 9), which alters the numbering of subsequent psalms in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles. The patristic tradition often reads the "poor" and "fatherless" Christologically — as figures of Christ Himself, who identifies with the humble and afflicted. The "man of the earth" in v. 18 is sometimes read typologically as the Antichrist or the worldly power opposed to God's kingdom.

**Debated modern teachings:** No specific prosperity-gospel, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace readings of Psalm 10 were found in the sources searched. These movements typically do not produce verse-by-verse commentaries on the Psalms, and Psalm 10's themes of oppression, delayed justice, and the prosperity of the wicked sit uneasily with prosperity-gospel assumptions about immediate blessing for the righteous.
